# 

# **1\. Introduction** {#1.-introduction}

A shift scheduling system, with an extended notification system.

We are developing a system similar to Quinyx and Planday. It is not a system designed for a specific company, but rather a broad solution that can be used by many different companies that need shift scheduling across departments and organizations.

# **1.1 Problem description** {#1.1-problem-description}

“Shift happens” is in testing at Acme corp. Currently they’re facing slow system response time and availability because of increased employee usage of the system and the Monolithic deployment. It is currently a Layered Architecture, which limits scaling to vertical improvements. They’re reached a point where upgrading the server isn’t feasible anymore.

 The suggested course of action has been to divide the system into several stateless microservices and deploy them separately in order to scale horizontally.

# **1.3. Explanation of Choices for the Technology Stack** {#1.3.-explanation-of-choices-for-the-technology-stack}

The project will use a combination of different technologies to support the distributed architecture.

**Java 21 with Spring Boot 3.5** will be used for all backend microservices. It provides a stable and well-established environment for larger backend systems, the team already knows it, and the existing Shift Happens monolith is written in it, so business logic can be extracted into the new services instead of being rewritten.

**PostgreSQL** will be used as the relational database for the write side of every service, where strong consistency, transactions, constraints and clear relationships are important (for example the leave ledger and the transactional outbox). Each service has its own database.

**MongoDB** will be used for the read models (CQRS query side) of Scheduling and Leave, where documents shaped for the user interface avoid expensive joins.

**RabbitMQ** will be used as the message broker for asynchronous communication between microservices. This allows the services to exchange events without being tightly coupled.

**Kubernetes** will be used to deploy and orchestrate the containerized microservices in a production-like environment. It makes it possible to manage multiple services, scale them independently, restart failed containers, and support high availability.

Using one main language keeps the services consistent and lets every team member review every service, while the architecture itself (independent services, message broker, REST, GraphQL and containers) demonstrates interoperability, scalability and communication between independent services. The full stack is summarised below; further technologies may be added during the project.

| Concern | Choice | Why |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Backend services | Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5 | Known by the team; reuse of monolith code |
| REST API | Spring Web \+ springdoc-openapi | Swagger UI generated from the code and contract |
| GraphQL API | Spring for GraphQL | Schema-first read API for the schedule views |
| Messaging | RabbitMQ 4 (topic exchange) \+ Spring AMQP | Routing by event type, one queue per consumer, dead-letter queues |
| Write databases | PostgreSQL 17 \+ Flyway | Transactions, constraints, versioned migrations |
| Read databases | MongoDB 8 | UI-shaped documents for CQRS read models |
| Authentication | Spring Security, OAuth 2.0/OIDC (Google, GitHub), RS256 JWT | Standard login flow; one token format for all services |
| API gateway | Caddy (local), NGINX Ingress (Kubernetes) | TLS and routing only, no business logic |
| Frontend | React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Apollo Client | Existing frontend; Apollo for GraphQL, fetch for REST |
| Containers / orchestration | Docker, Docker Compose, Kubernetes (kind/minikube), Kustomize, Helm | Development with Compose, production-like with Kubernetes |
| Serverless / autoscaling | KEDA (ScaledJob, ScaledObject), HPA | Scale-to-zero jobs and queue-based scaling |
| Observability | OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Grafana | Vendor-neutral metrics, logs and traces |
| CI/CD and quality | GitHub Actions, JUnit 5, Testcontainers, SonarQube Cloud, CodeQL, Trivy | Automated tests and static analysis on every pull request |

 

# **2\. System Architecture** {#2.-system-architecture}

## **2.0.1 System Architecture Design** {#2.0.1-system-architecture-design}

Initially, we divided our architecture into services based on intuition rather than using any formal domain analysis techniques. This resulted in several candidate services, but as we refined the design, we discovered two useful approaches for identifying bounded contexts: Event Storming and Historical Modelling. These techniques helped us define more meaningful microservice boundaries.

Before applying these methods, we considered several additional service splits. The Leave service was initially designed to be divided into a dedicated Leave Ledger service, isolating the write model as part of a CQRS-inspired architecture. Similarly, we explored separating Shift Swap from the Scheduling service to isolate its command and query responsibilities. We also considered moving Department and Workplace into their own service, separate from Employee, since these entities change relatively infrequently and have different lifecycle characteristics. 

However, these proposed splits would have introduced additional inter-service communication and increased overall system complexity without providing sufficient domain value. After further analysis, we decided against creating these artificial boundaries. Rather than splitting existing domains simply to meet the requirement of having at least five microservices, we introduced a dedicated Notification service. This allowed us to preserve coherent domain boundaries while still satisfying the architectural requirements.

## **Event Storming** {#event-storming}

To validate our service boundaries, we used Event Storming, a domain-driven design technique that models a system around the business events that occur within it. Rather than starting from database tables or technical layers, Event Storming focuses on what happens in the business and how different parts of the system react to those events. This made it easier to identify natural bounded contexts and the responsibilities of each microservice.

The resulting event storm illustrates how the services collaborate through asynchronous, event-driven communication. Each domain owns its own data and publishes events whenever its state changes. Other services subscribe to the events they are interested in, reducing direct dependencies while keeping the system loosely coupled.

From this process, we identified five bounded contexts that represent distinct business capabilities:

1. Authentication – Manages user identities, login, roles, and authorization.  
2. Scheduling – Handles shifts, schedules, and shift swap requests.  
3. Leave Service – Manages leave requests, approvals, and leave balances.  
4. Workforce – Maintains employee, department, and workplace information.  
5. Notifications – Delivers emails and in-app notifications in response to events generated by the other services.

A key outcome of the workshop was recognizing that Notifications is a supporting domain rather than a core business domain. Instead of embedding notification logic into every service, all domains simply publish events (e.g., `LeaveApproved` or `ShiftSwapAccepted`), and the Notification service independently decides how and when to notify users. This keeps the core services focused on their own business responsibilities.

### **Event Storm legend** {#event-storm-legend}

* 🔴 Red: Domain events (facts that have already happened)  
* 🟡 Yellow: Aggregates and business entities  
* 🔵 Blue: Commands that trigger business actions  
* 🟣 Purple: Bounded contexts / microservice domains

The event storm served as the primary justification for our microservice decomposition, ensuring that service boundaries were driven by business behavior rather than technical implementation details.

![][image2]

## **Historical Model** {#historical-model}

After identifying our bounded contexts through Event Storming, we used a Historical Model to validate how those domains interact over time. A historical model maps the chronological sequence of business events, allowing us to understand dependencies between domains and ensure that responsibilities are placed in the correct service.

Rather than focusing on individual commands, this model follows the lifecycle of an employee from onboarding to day-to-day operations. It highlights which events must occur before others and shows how each microservice contributes to the overall business process through published events.

The timeline begins with the creation of an Employee in the Workforce service. Before the employee can participate in operational workflows, a Department and Workplace must exist, and the employee must be assigned a valid Contract. Only after these prerequisite events have occurred can the Scheduling service create shifts or the Leave service process leave requests.

This chronological view helped confirm that our chosen service boundaries reflect real business dependencies rather than artificial technical separations. It also demonstrates how the system coordinates workflows through asynchronous events instead of tightly coupled service calls.

### **What the timeline shows** {#what-the-timeline-shows}

1. Workforce creates the employee and organizational structure.  
2. Contract is assigned, making the employee eligible for work.  
3. Scheduling creates and manages shifts.  
4. Leave Service processes leave requests and approvals.  
5. Notifications reacts to events throughout the timeline to inform users.

The historical model complements the Event Storm by answering a different question: Event Storming identifies who owns what, while the Historical Model shows when interactions occur and how business processes flow across the microservices.

## **2.1. Introduction to the microservices architecture** {#2.1.-introduction-to-the-microservices-architecture}

Shift Happens is split into **seven backend microservices**, each owning one business capability and its own data. We started from the business workflows in the event storm and grouped responsibilities that change together and share the same data:

| Workflow | Service | Owns |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Log in | Identity | Accounts, password hashes, external logins, JWT signing keys |
| Maintain staff | Workforce | Employees, contracts, departments, job roles, work locations |
| Plan the week | Scheduling | Shifts, required job roles, assignments, approvals and shift swaps |
| Take time off | Leave | Leave types, requests, approvals, immutable leave ledger |
| Cover a gap | AI | AI replacement suggestions for understaffed shifts |
| Stay informed | Notification | In-app notifications (email is sent by a serverless function) |
| Trace changes | Audit | Append-only log of every business event |

 

The frontend, the API gateway, the databases, RabbitMQ, the LLM and the serverless email function are not counted as microservices.

**Communication styles.** The React frontend talks only to the API gateway: **REST** (/api/v1/...) for all commands and most reads, and **GraphQL** (/api/graphql) for the schedule views of the Scheduling service. The gateway terminates TLS and routes by path; it contains no business logic. Between microservices there are **no synchronous calls**: services communicate only through **RabbitMQ events**, and a service that needs another service's data keeps a local copy built from those events.

*\[Insert the high-level architecture diagram here: docs/shift-happens-high-level-architecture.drawio in the repository.\]*

**AI use case.** When a shift becomes understaffed, for example because approved leave removes an employee from a shift, the Scheduling service publishes an event containing the relevant shift information and a list of qualified and available employees. A dedicated AI service sends this information to a cloud-based AI model, which ranks the candidates and provides a short justification for each suggestion. The result is then published back to the system and presented to the manager in the scheduling interface.

The manager can review the AI-generated suggestions and manually assign an employee to the shift through a REST request. The AI service never changes the schedule directly. Its output is validated before being used, and the system can fall back to a rule-based ranking if the AI service is unavailable or does not return a valid response.

The system uses relational databases for persistent data storage. Data ownership is separated between the individual services, while communication between services is handled through REST APIs and asynchronous messaging.

All contracts between the frontend and the services, as well as between the services themselves, are stored in the contracts/ folder of the repository. This includes OpenAPI specifications for REST endpoints and an AsyncAPI document describing the system's asynchronous events.

## **2.2. Microservices Description** {#2.2.-microservices-description}

Each service is described by its purpose, APIs, events, data, key business logic and behaviour under load or failure. The detailed API specifications are in the contracts/ folder and are referenced rather than duplicated here.

### **Identity Service** {#identity-service}

●      **Purpose:** Authenticates users with local credentials or Google/GitHub (OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect) and issues the JWT used by all other services. It is isolated because it is security-critical and changes for different reasons than the business services; other services only depend on its public key.  
●      **APIs:** REST: login, OIDC authorize/callback, set password. Internally it publishes its public key (JWKS). REST fits simple request/response and the redirect-based OAuth flow.  
●      **Events:** Consumes workforce.employee.created/updated/deleted to create, update or disable the login account. Publishes none.  
●      **Data:** PostgreSQL: accounts, hashed passwords, links to external identities and signing keys. Relational because of unique constraints (e-mail, external subject).  
●      **Business logic:** External logins are only accepted if the provider's verified e-mail belongs to an existing, active employee account. Deactivated employees cannot log in. Tokens carry employeeId and role.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** Stateless apart from its database and horizontally scalable. If it is down, no new logins are possible, but existing tokens stay valid because other services verify them with the cached public key.

### **Workforce Service** {#workforce-service}

●      **Purpose:** Master data about employees and the organisation. It is the single source of truth that other services replicate.  
●      **APIs:** REST CRUD for employees, contracts, employee job roles, departments, job roles and work locations; plain CRUD does not need GraphQL.  
●      **Events:** Publishes workforce.employee.created/updated/deleted with a full snapshot of the employee (including job roles) and a tombstone on delete. Consumes none.  
●      **Data:** PostgreSQL with relational constraints. Salary and other sensitive fields never leave the service.  
●      **Business logic:** Validation of employee data, deactivation, and job-role qualifications with expiry dates.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** Low write volume. If Workforce is down, other services keep working with their local replicas. Events are kept in its outbox until the broker is reachable.

### **Scheduling Service (CQRS)** {#scheduling-service-(cqrs)}

●      **Purpose:** Shifts, required job roles, assignments, shift approvals and shift swaps. Swaps belong here because they only change assignments that Scheduling already owns.  
●      **APIs:** Command role: REST for all writes (shifts, assignments, swaps, approvals). Query role: GraphQL for the schedule views, because the UI needs nested data (shift → assignments → employees → AI suggestions) in one request.  
●      **Events:** Publishes scheduling.shift.\*, scheduling.assignment.\*, scheduling.swap.\*, scheduling.shift.understaffed and the saga replies scheduling.leave-release.completed/rejected. Consumes workforce.employee.\* (local replica), leave.request.approval-started (saga step) and ai.replacement.suggested (read model).  
●      **Data:** Command side: PostgreSQL write model, outbox and employee replica. Query side: MongoDB documents shaped for the schedule views.  
●      **Business logic:** No overlapping shifts per employee; only qualified, active employees can be assigned; an approved swap reassigns the shift in one transaction; approved leave releases overlapping assignments unless a shift is locked (starts within 24 hours); understaffed shifts trigger a suggestion request with pre-filtered candidates.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** The query role scales independently of the command role. If the command role is down, schedules can still be read (A-04). If the query role is down, writes are still accepted and the read model catches up from its queue.

### **Leave Service (CQRS, saga orchestrator)** {#leave-service-(cqrs,-saga-orchestrator)}

●      **Purpose:** Leave types, leave requests, approvals and the immutable leave ledger. It orchestrates the leave-approval saga. It is isolated because leave has its own rules and an audit-sensitive balance history.  
●      **APIs:** REST for requests, approvals, leave types and ledger entries (read and append only). The gateway sends GET requests to the query role and all other requests to the command role.  
●      **Events:** Publishes leave.request.submitted/approval-started/approved/rejected and leave.ledger.entry-recorded. Consumes scheduling.leave-release.completed/rejected (saga replies) and workforce.employee.\* (local replica).  
●      **Data:** Command side: PostgreSQL with requests, the append-only ledger, balance snapshots, the saga table and the outbox. Query side: MongoDB with balances and overviews.  
●      **Business logic:** Balance check before approval; approval reserves days in the ledger and starts the saga; completion or compensation depending on the Scheduling reply or a timeout.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** If Scheduling is unavailable, the saga message waits durably in the queue; when the saga times out, Leave compensates, so no request stays half-approved. The balance can always be rebuilt from the immutable ledger.

### **AI Service** {#ai-service}

●      **Purpose:** Suggests replacements for understaffed shifts. It is isolated so that the latency and failures of the language model never affect the core workflows, and so the model can be replaced independently.  
●      **APIs:** No public API apart from its health endpoint; the suggestions reach the frontend through the Scheduling GraphQL API.  
●      **Events:** Consumes scheduling.shift.understaffed. Publishes ai.replacement.suggested.  
●      **Data:** PostgreSQL: processed event ids, generated suggestions and a prompt/response log for review.  
●      **Business logic:** Builds the prompt from the candidates in the event, validates that the model returns only candidates from the input, and falls back to a rule-based ranking (fewest hours this week) on timeout or invalid output. It is advisory only.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** The LLM is the slowest component, so requests are buffered in the queue and consumers can be scaled on queue length (KEDA). Failures lead to the rule-based fallback, never to a blocked workflow.

### **Notification Service** {#notification-service}

●      **Purpose:** Informs users about assignments, cancelled shifts, swaps, leave decisions and AI suggestions. As a fan-out subscriber, new notification types can be added without changing the producers.  
●      **APIs:** REST: list notifications for the logged-in user and mark them as read (the frontend polls).  
●      **Events:** Consumes the relevant scheduling, leave and AI events. Publishes notification.email.requested, which the serverless email function sends.  
●      **Data:** PostgreSQL with notifications per employee.  
●      **Business logic:** Maps each event to its recipients and message; de-duplicates by event id.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** If it is down, events wait in its own queue and no other service is affected. Email sending is offloaded to the serverless function.

### **Audit Service** {#audit-service}

●      **Purpose:** Keeps a complete, append-only history of all business events so administrators can trace who did what and when (F-10). It is isolated because its load is write-heavy and read-rare.  
●      **APIs:** REST: search the audit log (administrators only), filterable by event type, entity and correlation id.  
●      **Events:** Consumes all workforce, scheduling, leave and AI events. Publishes none.  
●      **Data:** PostgreSQL append-only table with the original event envelopes and a unique constraint on the event id.  
●      **Business logic:** Stores every event unchanged; a redelivered event is ignored.  
●      **Scaling and failure:** Never on the critical path; a backlog is simply processed later.

In addition, the **email function** is a serverless task (not a microservice): it consumes notification.email.requested and sends e-mails over SMTP. In Kubernetes it runs as a KEDA ScaledJob that scales to zero when the queue is empty.

## **2.3. Communication between microservices** {#2.3.-communication-between-microservices}

| From → To | Style | Used for |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Browser → API gateway | HTTPS | Single entry point with TLS termination |
| Frontend → services | REST /api/v1/... | All commands, and reads for Identity, Workforce, Leave, Notification and Audit |
| Frontend → Scheduling | GraphQL /api/graphql | Schedule views with nested data in one request |
| Service → service | RabbitMQ events | All integration between services; no synchronous calls |
| Identity → Google/GitHub | OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect | Third-party login |
| AI → OpenRouter | HTTP (AI API) | Language model inference |
| Email function → SMTP | SMTP | E-mail delivery (Mailpit locally) |

 

**Frontend interaction.** A typical page uses both API styles. The manager's week view loads the shifts, assignments, employee names and AI suggestions with one GraphQL query. Assigning a suggested employee is a REST call (POST /api/v1/shiftassignments), and the view is refreshed through GraphQL. Every POST carries an Idempotency-Key header, so a retried click cannot create duplicates.

**Why no synchronous calls between services.** If Scheduling called Workforce on every assignment, a Workforce outage would stop scheduling as well. Instead, Workforce publishes a full snapshot of every employee change, and Scheduling and Leave keep a local replica. The cost is that the replica is eventually consistent, normally less than a second behind.

**Events.** All events are published to one topic exchange (shift-happens.events) with the event type as routing key, for example scheduling.swap.approved.v1.

●      Every message uses the same envelope: eventId, eventType, aggregateId, aggregateVersion, occurredAt, correlationId and causationId, with the entity snapshot in data.  
●      Each consuming service owns one durable queue bound to exactly the event types it needs. Several replicas of the same service share that queue as competing consumers.  
●      Failed messages are retried and then moved to a dead-letter exchange.  
●      Producers use a transactional outbox, so a state change and its event are never out of sync.  
●      All events, queues, producers and consumers are documented in AsyncAPI (contracts/asyncapi.yaml).

**Security.** Identity signs JWTs with RS256. Every service validates the token itself with Identity's public key and enforces the role rules for its own operations, because it owns the business rules. The gateway only routes.

## **2.4. Description of the patterns and techniques used in the project** {#2.4.-description-of-the-patterns-and-techniques-used-in-the-project}

The table gives an overview of the patterns and where they are applied. The following subsections explain each of them.

| Pattern | Where | Why |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CQRS | Scheduling, Leave | Read-heavy, nested views vs. transactional writes |
| Snapshot pattern | All events; leave balance snapshots | Consumers never call back; fast balances |
| Tombstone pattern | Deletes of employees, shifts, assignments | Deleted entities cannot be resurrected by late events |
| Immutable ledger | Leave ledger | Full history; corrections are new entries |
| Idempotency | All REST POSTs; all event consumers | Retries never cause duplicate side effects |
| Commutative handlers (Important) | All read models and replicas | Message order does not change the result |
| Saga (orchestrated) | Leave approval across Leave and Scheduling | Consistency without distributed transactions |
| Transactional outbox (Overkill?) | Every event producer | State change and event are committed together |
| Serverless function (Overkill?) | Email function (KEDA ScaledJob) | Isolated, bursty background work that scales to zero |
| Caching | JWT public key; GraphQL responses (planned) | Fewer repeated lookups and queries |

 

### **2.4.1. CQRS** {#2.4.1.-cqrs}

Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) can improve scalability when read and write operations have significantly different requirements. For example, an Audit Log may receive a large number of writes because every action needs to be recorded, while reads are relatively rare. In this case, separating the read and write models allows each side to be optimized independently.

Another example is a Shift service, where many users may frequently search, filter, and page through shifts. A document database can be used for the read model to avoid expensive joins and optimize these read-heavy operations, while a relational database can handle writes where strong consistency, relationships, and constraints are important. Changes to the relational database can then be propagated asynchronously to the document database, keeping the read model up to date.

In Shift Happens, CQRS is applied to the **Scheduling** and **Leave** services. Each is one codebase deployed twice: a command role with a PostgreSQL write model, and a query role with a MongoDB read model that is updated asynchronously from events. Scheduling's query role serves GraphQL, because the schedule views need nested data; Leave's query role serves REST GET requests for balances and overviews. Reads and writes scale independently, and reads stay available when the write side is down. The price is eventual consistency and more moving parts, which is why CQRS is not used for simple CRUD services such as Identity and Workforce, nor for Audit, which only appends and rarely reads.

### **2.4.2. Immutable data (Tombstone pattern and Snapshot pattern)** {#2.4.2.-immutable-data-(tombstone-pattern-and-snapshot-pattern)}

**Immutable leave ledger.** Ledger entries are never updated or deleted. A correction, and the compensation in the leave saga, is a new REVERSAL entry with the opposite amount, which gives a complete history of every balance change.

**Snapshot pattern.** Every event carries a full snapshot of the entity after the change, not just a diff, so consumers can store it directly and never need to call the producer. In addition, the Leave service stores a balance snapshot for each employee and leave type every 50 ledger entries, so a balance is the latest snapshot plus the entries after it instead of a sum over the whole history.

**Tombstone pattern.** Deletes are soft (the row is marked as deleted) and publish a \*.deleted.v1 tombstone event. Consumers keep the tombstone instead of removing the record, so a late, out-of-order update can never bring a deleted employee, shift or assignment back to life.

### **2.4.3. Idempotence** {#2.4.3.-idempotence}

**Client requests.** Every REST POST requires an Idempotency-Key header that the frontend generates once per user action. The service stores the key with its first response for 24 hours. A repeated request returns the stored response without a second side effect, and reusing a key with a different body is rejected with 409\. PUT, PATCH and DELETE are idempotent by definition.

**Messages.** RabbitMQ delivers at least once, so every consumer stores the ids of processed events in the same transaction as its own change and ignores duplicates. A redelivered leave approval therefore cannot reserve days twice, and a redelivered e-mail request is not sent twice.

### **2.4.4. Commutative message handlers** {#2.4.4.-commutative-message-handlers}

Events may arrive out of order, for example after a retry or with several consumer replicas. Handlers are written so that the final state does not depend on the order:

●      Snapshot upserts keep the version with the highest aggregateVersion and ignore older ones.  
●      A tombstone wins over any lower version.  
●      Balances are sums of ledger entries, and addition is order-independent.

A test applies the same events in shuffled order and checks that the read model ends in the same state.

### **2.4.5. Saga pattern** {#2.4.5.-saga-pattern}

Approving leave must also release the employee's overlapping shifts, which are owned by another service. A distributed transaction across two databases is neither possible nor desirable, so the **leave-approval saga** keeps both services consistent with compensating actions. It is orchestrated by the Leave service:

●      The manager approves. In one local transaction, Leave sets the request to APPROVAL\_PENDING, appends a RESERVATION ledger entry and publishes leave.request.approval-started.  
●      Scheduling releases the employee's overlapping assignments and replies with scheduling.leave-release.completed. If a shift is locked (it starts within 24 hours or has been checked into), it changes nothing and replies with scheduling.leave-release.rejected.  
●      On completed, Leave marks the request APPROVED. On rejected, or if no reply arrives before the timeout, Leave compensates: it appends a REVERSAL ledger entry and marks the request REJECTED with the reason.

Orchestration was chosen over choreography because one service then holds the saga state, the timeout and the compensation logic, which makes it easier to test and explain. Released shifts trigger the AI replacement suggestion.

### **2.4.6. Caching** {#2.4.6.-caching}

Every service caches Identity's public key, so tokens are validated without a network call. The CQRS read models act as a pre-computed cache of the views. A short-lived cache of GraphQL schedule responses per user is planned if load tests show it is needed. Caches are never used for write decisions.

### **2.4.7. Transactional outbox** {#2.4.7.-transactional-outbox}

A service must not update its database and then fail before publishing the event, or the other way around. Producers therefore write each event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, and a relay publishes it to RabbitMQ afterwards. Together with idempotent consumers this gives effectively-once processing.

### **2.4.8. Serverless function** {#2.4.8.-serverless-function}

Sending e-mails is an isolated, bursty background task. It runs as a short-lived job (email-function) that drains the email queue and exits. In local Kubernetes it is a KEDA ScaledJob triggered by the queue length, so it uses no resources when there is nothing to send.

# **3\. Environments description** {#3.-environments-description}

## **Deployment Strategy**

At this stage of the project, the deployment strategy is still being planned. The main goal is to create an architecture that can run locally during development and later be moved to a cloud environment with as few changes as possible.

The system will consist of multiple containerized microservices, databases, RabbitMQ, and a frontend application. Docker will be used to package the individual services, while Docker Compose will be used for the local development environment. Kubernetes will later be used to simulate a production-like environment and manage deployment, scaling, and service availability.

This follows the project requirement that development should use Docker Compose and that a local Kubernetes environment should simulate production.

We initially considered several cloud providers:

* Railway  
* Amazon Web Services (AWS)  
* Google Cloud Platform (GCP)

Our initial plan is to use Railway as the primary cloud platform. Railway provides a simple deployment workflow for containerized applications and includes managed services such as PostgreSQL, networking, environment variable management, and automatic deployments from GitHub. Its developer-friendly experience and generous free/student tier make it well suited for this project.

A possible cloud setup could include:

* Railway Services for deploying the containerized microservices.  
* Railway PostgreSQL with one database per microservice for the relational write models.  
* MongoDB Atlas for the read models of Scheduling and Leave.  
* RabbitMQ deployed as a separate Railway service using the official Docker image.  
* The frontend deployed as its own Railway service with automatic deployments.

The final deployment architecture may change during the project as we evaluate cost, scalability, and operational complexity. However, by containerizing all services with Docker, the application remains portable and can be migrated to another cloud provider with minimal changes if needed.

In the previous Shift Happens project, cloud-hosted PostgreSQL, MongoDB Atlas, and Neo4j AuraDB were already evaluated as managed services, providing useful experience that can be applied to this deployment strategy.

## **3.1. Development environment with Docker Compose** {#3.1.-development-environment-with-docker-compose}

The development environment is defined in docker-compose.microservices.yml. The existing docker-compose.yml still runs the monolith while services are extracted.

●      **Infrastructure** (started by default): one PostgreSQL per service, MongoDB for the two read models, RabbitMQ with its management UI, Mailpit as a local e-mail inbox, and the OpenTelemetry Collector.  
●      **Profile app:** all microservices, the frontend, the serverless email function, and Caddy as the API gateway on https\://localhost:8443.  
●      **Profile ai:** the LLM and a one-shot container that downloads the model.  
●      **Networks** mirror the production security boundaries: databases sit on internal networks reachable only by their owning service, services share an internal service-bus network, and only the gateway is exposed.  
●      Every service exposes GET /health, which Compose uses for health checks.

 

## **3.2. Local Kubernetes deployment simulating a production-like environment** {#3.2.-local-kubernetes-deployment-simulating-a-production-like-environment}

The production-like environment is a local Kubernetes cluster (kind or minikube). The manifests live in the k8s/ folder:

●      A Kustomize base with a Deployment and a Service per service role (Scheduling and Leave have separate command and query Deployments).  
●      Readiness and liveness probes on /health, and shared configuration in a ConfigMap. Secrets such as database passwords and OIDC client secrets come from Kubernetes Secrets and are never committed.  
●      An NGINX Ingress with the same routing rules as the local gateway.  
●      Infrastructure (ingress controller, KEDA, RabbitMQ, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Ollama, observability stack) is installed with Helm charts.

*\[Insert the Kubernetes deployment diagram here.\]*

### **3.2.1. Description of used technologies** {#3.2.1.-description-of-used-technologies}

Kubernetes orchestrates the containers, restarts failed instances and performs rolling updates. Kustomize keeps one base configuration with an overlay per environment. Helm installs third-party infrastructure with pinned chart versions. KEDA adds event-driven autoscaling and scale-to-zero jobs. Images are stored in GitHub Container Registry.

### **3.2.2. CI/CD pipeline description and diagram** {#3.2.2.-ci/cd-pipeline-description-and-diagram}

The CI/CD pipeline uses GitHub Actions in the monorepo. Path filters make sure that only the services affected by a change are built:

●      Build and unit tests (JUnit 5).  
●      Static analysis: SonarQube Cloud quality gate and CodeQL for security issues. The contract files (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL, JSON Schema) are linted on every change.  
●      Integration tests with Testcontainers: the service with its real database and RabbitMQ.  
●      System-level cooperation tests: two or more services and RabbitMQ in containers.  
●      Build the container image and scan it with Trivy.  
●      On main: push the image to GitHub Container Registry, tagged with the version and git SHA, and deploy to the local cluster with a smoke test.

Any failing step fails the pipeline, and pull requests can only be merged into main when the pipeline is green.

*\[Insert the CI/CD pipeline diagram here.\]*

### **3.2.3. Logging and Monitoring** {#3.2.3.-logging-and-monitoring}

Because the application consists of multiple microservices, centralized logging and monitoring will be important.

Every service is instrumented with OpenTelemetry and sends traces, metrics and logs to the OpenTelemetry Collector (already part of the Compose setup). In Kubernetes the collector forwards them to **Prometheus** (metrics), **Loki** (logs) and **Tempo** (traces), visualised in **Grafana**. The correlation id travels with every request and event, so one user action can be followed across REST calls, RabbitMQ and all services.

We plan to monitor request rate, errors and latency per service, queue depth and dead-letter queues, saga timeouts and the AI fallback rate. Alternatives considered were the ELK stack (heavier to run), Jaeger (traces only) and managed services such as Azure Monitor or Grafana Cloud. Because the collector is vendor-neutral, switching only requires changing its exporter.

 

### **3.2.4. Autoscaling configuration** {#3.2.4.-autoscaling-configuration}

●      **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** on the query roles (Scheduling and Leave): 1 to 5 replicas at 70% CPU, because read traffic dominates.  
●      **KEDA ScaledObjects** on queue consumers (for example the AI service), scaling on RabbitMQ queue length.  
●      **KEDA ScaledJob** for the email function: 0 jobs when the queue is empty, up to 5 when messages pile up.  
●      Critical services run with at least two replicas in production (A-01). Command roles scale more conservatively because their databases are the limit.

## **3.3. Cloud deployment plan** {#3.3.-cloud-deployment-plan}

No actual cloud deployment is required. Building on the Deployment Strategy above, our plan maps the local setup to Microsoft Azure as follows:

| Local component | Azure service |
| :---- | :---- |
| Kubernetes (kind/minikube) | Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) across availability zones |
| Container images | Azure Container Registry (or GitHub Container Registry) |
| PostgreSQL per service | Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server (zone-redundant HA, automated backups) |
| MongoDB read models | MongoDB Atlas or Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB |
| RabbitMQ | RabbitMQ cluster in AKS with quorum queues, or a hosted RabbitMQ (CloudAMQP) |
| Caddy / NGINX Ingress | Application Gateway for Containers or NGINX Ingress with a public IP |
| Secrets | Azure Key Vault |
| Observability | Azure Managed Grafana \+ Azure Monitor (Prometheus), or the same Grafana stack in AKS |
| Mailpit | Azure Communication Services Email |
| Ollama | GPU node pool, or a hosted model (Azure OpenAI) behind the same AI service |

   
●      **Scalability:** stateless services scale out with HPA and KEDA, and read and write sides scale separately. Databases scale up, and the read models can use read replicas.  
●      **Availability:** at least two replicas per critical service, spread over zones, zone-redundant managed databases, rolling updates, and durable queues that buffer during outages.  
●      **Security and data management:** TLS at the ingress, network policies that mirror the Compose networks, secrets in Key Vault, and backups and point-in-time restore from the managed databases.  
●      **Deployment and release:** images tagged with version and SHA, rolling updates, and database migrations run by each service at startup.  
●      **Pricing:** we start from student credits and free tiers with small instance sizes, and scale-to-zero functions. The language model is the main cost driver, so a hosted model with pay-per-use may be cheaper than a GPU node at low volume.  
●      **Trade-offs:** managed databases and a managed message broker cost more but remove operational work. A single region keeps latency and cost low; geographic distribution is not needed initially.

# **4\. Testing** {#4.-testing}

## **4.1. Testing strategy and scope** {#4.1.-testing-strategy-and-scope}

### **Initial Testing Strategy** {#initial-testing-strategy}

Testing will be introduced continuously while the microservices are developed rather than added only at the end of the project.

**Unit tests** will be used to test the business logic inside individual microservices. For example, the Scheduling service tests whether an employee is qualified and available before a shift swap or assignment is accepted.

**Integration tests** will test communication with external components such as databases, APIs, and RabbitMQ. Testcontainers could be used to start temporary database or RabbitMQ containers during the tests.

**System-level cooperation tests** will test whether multiple microservices work correctly together.

A cooperation test starts the Leave and Scheduling services with RabbitMQ in containers, approves a leave request and verifies both outcomes of the leave-approval saga: the shifts are released, or the approval is compensated when a shift is locked.

For this project, we therefore plan to include integration and cooperation testing from the beginning.

## **4.2. Unit testing** {#4.2.-unit-testing}

Every microservice has unit tests (JUnit 5, Mockito) for its core business rules, for example swap eligibility, overlapping shifts, the ledger balance calculation, the saga state machine and validation of the AI output. The domain layer is plain Java, so these tests run fast without Spring.

## **4.3. Integration testing** {#4.3.-integration-testing}

●      **REST/GraphQL API:** controllers tested with security enabled, including the Idempotency-Key replay behaviour.  
●      **Messaging:** Testcontainers RabbitMQ, checking that an event written to the outbox is published and processed by a consumer.  
●      **Database:** Testcontainers PostgreSQL and MongoDB, checking that the Flyway migrations and repositories work against the real database engines.

## **4.4. System-level cooperation testing** {#4.4.-system-level-cooperation-testing}

Cooperation tests start two or more real service containers with RabbitMQ and their databases, and verify that they cooperate through messaging, not through the UI. The first test covers the leave-approval saga (both outcomes). Further tests cover the AI replacement flow with a stubbed LLM, and replication of employees from Workforce to the other services.

## **4.5. Security testing focusing on verifying correct authentication and authorization** {#4.5.-security-testing-focusing-on-verifying-correct-authentication-and-authorization}

Automated tests check that a missing, expired or forged JWT returns 401, that a role without permission gets 403 (for example an employee calling a manager endpoint or the audit log), and that an OIDC login with an unknown e-mail is refused.

## **4.6. Static analysis and static testing to identify code quality or security issues** {#4.6.-static-analysis-and-static-testing-to-identify-code-quality-or-security-issues}

SonarQube Cloud (quality gate), CodeQL (security analysis of Java and TypeScript), Trivy (vulnerabilities in images and dependencies) and Dependabot (dependency updates) run automatically. The API and event contracts are also validated in CI.

## **4.7. Test execution in CI/CD** {#4.7.-test-execution-in-ci/cd}

All tests run in GitHub Actions on every pull request and on main (see 3.2.2). Integration and cooperation tests use Testcontainers on the hosted runners. Any failing test fails the pipeline and blocks the merge.

## **4.8. Limitations, risks, and trade-offs** {#4.8.-limitations,-risks,-and-trade-offs}

Cooperation tests are slower than unit tests, so they cover the most important flows rather than every combination. Real LLM output is not deterministic, so tests use a stubbed model, and the real model is only checked manually. End-to-end UI tests are out of scope for this course.

# **5\. Project Management and Team Collaboration** {#5.-project-management-and-team-collaboration}

## **5.1. Introduction to Project Management and Team Collaboration** {#5.1.-introduction-to-project-management-and-team-collaboration}

For this project, we use a **Scrum-inspired agile approach**. We do not follow the Scrum framework strictly, but we use several of its principles to organize the work and collaborate as a team.

The goal is to work iteratively, divide the project into smaller tasks, and continuously coordinate progress within the group.

 Waterfall does not fit microservices well because requirements and service boundaries often need to evolve during development. Microservices benefit from frequent feedback, testing, and independent changes, which aligns better with Agile and iterative development. Waterfall makes late architectural changes more expensive and difficult.

## **5.2. Methods Used During the Project** {#5.2.-methods-used-during-the-project}

We divide the project into smaller tasks and work in short iterations.

Tasks are planned and discussed as a group, and responsibilities are distributed between the team members. We regularly review the current progress, discuss problems, and adjust the plan when needed.

We use GitHub Issues and a GitHub Projects board (Backlog → In progress → Review → Done) to keep track of tasks, priorities and progress. The tasks are derived from the course requirements in a project plan (docs/project-plan.md) and grouped into work packages. We work in two-week iterations.

Every change goes through a pull request that needs a green CI pipeline and at least one review. Changes to the shared contracts (contracts/ folder) must be reviewed by the owners of every affected service. Because the contracts are agreed first, the services can be developed in parallel.

Each microservice has one owner and a backup. The owner reviews all changes to it and its contracts:

| Area | Owner | Backup |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Identity service and security tests | TBD | TBD |
| Workforce service | TBD | TBD |
| Scheduling service (REST commands \+ GraphQL query) | TBD | TBD |
| Leave service and saga | TBD | TBD |
| AI service and Ollama | TBD | TBD |
| Notification service, Audit service, email function | TBD | TBD |
| Frontend (REST \+ GraphQL \+ OIDC login) | TBD | TBD |
| CI/CD, Kubernetes and monitoring | TBD | TBD |

 

## **5.3. Versioning Strategies** {#5.3.-versioning-strategies}

We use **Git and GitHub** for source code versioning.

Changes are made in separate branches and merged into the main branch through pull requests when possible. This makes it easier to see who has contributed to the project and to review changes before they are merged.

Database changes will be versioned using migration scripts, and REST APIs will use a clear versioning strategy, for example `/api/v1/...`.

Concretely:  
●      **Source code:** Git monorepo with short-lived feature branches and pull requests; semantic-version tags per service (for example scheduling-service/v1.2.0).  
●      **Container images:** tagged with the version and the git SHA; never latest in Kubernetes.  
●      **Databases:** Flyway migrations per service (V1\_\_init.sql, …), forward-only and run at startup. MongoDB read models are rebuilt from events instead of migrated.  
●      **REST APIs:** URL versioning (/api/v1/...). Additive changes stay in v1; a breaking change gets /v2 alongside v1 until the frontend has moved.  
●      **GraphQL:** not versioned by design; fields are added and old ones marked @deprecated.  
●      **Events:** the version is part of the event type (for example leave.request.approved.v1); a breaking change publishes .v2 in parallel until all consumers have migrated.

## **5.4. Documentation Strategy** {#5.4.-documentation-strategy}

Documentation will be updated continuously during the project instead of only being written at the end.

The project will include:

●      A main README for the complete system.  
●      Documentation for each microservice.  
●      API documentation: Swagger/OpenAPI for REST, the GraphQL schema for GraphQL, and AsyncAPI for all events (kept in the contracts/ folder).  
●      Architecture diagrams.  
●      Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for important design decisions.

●      A project plan with work packages and tasks derived from the course requirements.

This should make it easier for all group members to understand the system and help new developers set up and work with the project.

6\. Discussion

6.1. Advantages and challenges of the distributed systems (application and database

perspectives)

6.2. Pros and cons of used patterns like CQRS etc.

6.3. Scalability / Autoscaling (application, messaging, and database perspectives)

6.4. Possible improvements

7\. Reflection: What was difficult about: designing the distributed system, project management, what design mistakes were made and fixed, what would be done differently next time, what you learned about databases in practice.

8\. Conclusion: short high-level summary of the project, results, main insights.

9\. References: All major design choices, technical claims, and comparisons must be supported by references. Sources must be cited in the text and listed in the References section. References should primarily be official documentation, textbooks, or academic or technical publications. Web tutorials and blogs may be used sparingly but should not be the primary sources. Use standard formats like APA, IEEE, or Harvard.
